All right, the last step I performed was to launch a fairly heavy background Python process that measures both training time-to-target and inference latency for the double‑decoder experiment. The tool call returned a background task ID (`bstyq4kjl`) and, crucially, the path where its stdout/stderr is being written:

`/tmp/claude-1000/-home-lane-MythosMini/189f0549-c2fc-4fc7-b50d-37cd255eabf2/tasks/bstyq4kjl.output`

The command is still running, and I need the actual numeric results before I can answer the user’s request to “measure efficiency (real time to result)”. Since the process is asynchronous, I cannot just `Read` the file – it may not be complete yet, and I would have to poll repeatedly. The environment provides a `Monitor` tool that can stream the output of a file in real time, essentially doing a `tail -f`. This is exactly what I need: it will block (up to a reasonable timeout) while the background process prints its JSON lines, and then return the captured output once the process finishes or the timeout expires.

I should set a timeout that’s generous enough for the training runs (they’re limited to 2400 steps for the 90% target, plus a separate inference benchmark). Empirically, the earlier test suite ran in ~3 seconds, but the new measurement script does full training loops and could take several minutes, especially on CPU (I forced `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""`). A 30‑minute window (1800000 ms) is more than sufficient; it also guards against an infinite hang.

The `persistent` flag determines whether the monitor should keep the file open after the timeout. I only need a single snapshot of the final output, so I’ll set `persistent: false` – once the command finishes or the timeout is reached, the tool will return the captured lines and close.

Thus, the next logical step is to invoke the `Monitor` tool with a `tail -f` command pointing at the output file, using the described timeout and non‑persistent mode. This will give me the JSON measurement results I need to report back to the user.
